title: Best, Average, and Worst Case Analysis

blocks.text: Have you ever wondered how to compare two algorithms without actually running them? Understanding best, average, and worst-case complexities is key to this comparison.

blocks.markdown: In algorithm analysis, we often need to predict how the performance of an algorithm scales with input size. This is where best, average, and worst-case complexities come into play. These concepts allow us to describe the efficiency of an algorithm in different scenarios.

blocks.title: Best-case Complexity
blocks.text: The best-case complexity of an algorithm is the minimum time or space required by the algorithm for any input of size $n$.

blocks.title: Average-case Complexity
blocks.text: The average-case complexity is the expected time or space required by the algorithm, averaged over all possible inputs of size $n$.

blocks.title: Worst-case Complexity
blocks.text: The worst-case complexity is the maximum time or space required by the algorithm for any input of size $n$.

blocks.markdown: To illustrate these concepts, consider the simple example of linear search. In the best case, the target element is the first element in the list, resulting in $O(1)$ complexity. In the average case, the target is somewhere in the middle, leading to $O(n)$ complexity. In the worst case, the target is the last element or not present at all, also resulting in $O(n)$ complexity.

blocks.title: Linear Search Complexity
blocks.prompt: Analyze the best, average, and worst-case complexities of linear search in an unsorted array.

steps.latex: The best-case occurs when the target element is the first element in the array, requiring only one comparison: $O(1)$.
Assume the target is equally likely to be at any position. On average, it will be in the middle of the array, requiring $n/2$ comparisons: $O(n)$.
The worst-case occurs when the target is the last element or not present, requiring $n$ comparisons: $O(n)$.

blocks.markdown: Now, let's explore amortised analysis, which provides a different perspective. Amortised analysis is used when an algorithm has operations that vary greatly in cost, but the average cost over a sequence of operations is more predictable.

blocks.title: Amortised Analysis
blocks.text: Amortised analysis calculates the average time per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations, providing a more realistic measure of an algorithm's performance in practice.

blocks.title: Dynamic Array Growth
blocks.prompt: Explain the amortised cost of appending an element to a dynamic array.

steps.text: Consider the cost of appending an element.
steps.latex: If the array has space, appending takes $O(1)$ time.

steps.text: Consider the cost when the array is full.
steps.latex: When full, the array is resized (typically doubled), and all elements are copied, taking $O(n)$ time.
Over $n$ operations, resizing happens infrequently. The total cost is $O(n)$ for $n$ appends, leading to an amortised cost of $O(1)$ per append.

blocks.answer: The amortised cost of appending to a dynamic array is $O(1)$.

rows: Average time per operation over sequence
blocks.caption: Comparison of Complexity Cases

blocks.markdown: When choosing which case to optimize for, consider the typical use case of the algorithm. If the worst-case scenario is unacceptable, prioritize optimizing for it. Otherwise, average-case performance might be more relevant.

blocks.title: Choosing the Right Case
blocks.text: Always consider the context in which an algorithm will be used to decide which complexity case to optimize for.

points: Best, average, and worst-case complexities provide a framework for analyzing an algorithm's performance.
Amortised analysis offers a practical view of performance over multiple operations.
Choose the case to optimize based on the application's requirements.
